newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria proposes currency board based at c.bank.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria proposes currency board based at c.bank.

text.p: Bulgaria's cabinet has proposed operating a currency board system suggested by the International Monetary Fund from its existing central bank by dividing it into two departments, government officials say.
Parliamentary speaker Blagovest Sendov and Prime Minister Zhan Videnov started a series of consultations with political parties and trade unions on the currency board and its alternatives on Tuesday.
"A central bank could be transformed into two departments, one of which would act as a currency board and the other one as a banking deparment," Finance Minister Dimitar Kostov told reporters.

The IMF has proposed introducing a currency board to stabilise the economy and halt the fall in the lev, which hit a new record low of 330 per dollar at midday on Wednesday from 283-285 at Tuesday's close on high dollar demand.

The proposal has raised fears over sovereignty and Bulgarian National Bank (BNB) governor Lyubomir Filipov has said that under BNB law he could not support a currency board if it ruled out the existence of the central bank.
Under the system, the amount of national currency in circulation must be exactly matched by the central bank's hard currency reserves, preventing the bank from printing money.

The question of who should run the board and how independent it would be from the politicians and bankers blamed for getting the economy into its present state has attracted even more speculation than the likely exchange rate at which the lev would be pegged.

The IMF has expressed concern that corruption is blocking implementation of reforms in Bulgaria. Parliament's commission against corruption last week issued a White Book which blamed uncontrolled siphoning of funds abroad.
The opposition Union of Democratic Forces says it will not support a currency board while the Socialists remain in power.
Currency boards, which usually peg a local currency to the dollar, have been used by countries such as Argentina, Estonia and Lithuania to restore confidence and defeat hyperinflation.
Once a consensus is reached, the proposal must be approved by parliament, where Videnov's Socialists have a majority.
Videnov said the government was preparing a two-year stabilisation programme which assumed a currency board would be set up.

He reassured investors that their Treasury paper would continue to be honoured. "There are no reasons for concern that maturity and coupon payments on state paper would be temporary suspended if Bulgaria imposed a currency board system," he told reporters.
